dataset.name: SPRUCE S1 Bog Pretreatment Photosynthesis and Respiration for Black Spruce: 2010-2013
description: This data set contains biochemical, morphological, and physiological data collected between 2010 and 2013 on mature black spruce (Picea mariana) trees at the S1 bog site in northern Minnesota, located 40 km north of Grand Rapids in the USDA Forest Service Marcell Experimental Forest (MEF). These data were collected prior to the initiating of heating and elevation of CO2 for the SPRUCE experiment to assess the response of northern peatland ecosystems to increases in temperature and exposures to elevated atmospheric CO2 concentrations.

Seasonal patterns of the photosynthetic capacity of current- (Y0) and one-year old (Y1) foliage were measured in April, May, July, September, August and October between 2010 and 2013. The potential influences of canopy position and needle age on photosynthesis were measured for three successive needle cohorts (Y0, Y1 and two-year old (Y2)) from top, middle and bottom branches in July 2011. Photosynthetic response (A/Ci) curves were produced using portable infrared gas analyzer systems (LI6400XT, Li-COR, USA). A/Ci curves were generated at saturating light levels (PAR > 1000 μmol m-2 s-1) by sequential adjustment of the reference CO2 concentration between 50 and 1600 ppm to assess A across a broad range of intercellular CO2 concentrations. Temperature response surfaces were generated by replication of the A/Ci curves at multiple temperatures.

measurementTechnique:
Site Description:
The research was conducted in a mixed peatland black spruce and Larix laricina [tamarack] stand at the Marcell Experimental Forest in northern Minnesota, USA. Elevation is 410 m above sea level. The stand was established by natural regeneration following two strip-cuttings in 1969 and 1974 (Sebestyen et al. 2011). The evaluated bog (S1-Bog) has an open canopy structure, with an average tree height of 4.5 m and a basal area of 5.6 cm2 m-2, February 2013. The understory consists of woody shrub species (e.g. Rhododendron groenlandicum [Labrador tea] and Chamaedaphne calyculata [leatherleaf]) and a ground layer of moss species (e.g. Sphagnum spp. and Polytrichum spp.) and herbaceous species (e.g. Eriophorum angustifolium [cotton grass] and Maianthemum trifolium [three-leaf false Solomon’s seal]).
The target species is black spruce. At the site, black spruce trees retain on average five foliar cohorts. Bud break occurs normally during June and the newly developed foliage (Y0), becomes fully expanded towards the end of July and beginning of August. Under normal conditions, black spruce produces one shoot (cohort) a year, but can flush again under favorable conditions. However, between 2010 and 2013 trees seem to flush only once (Anna M. Jensen, personal observation). Cohort age was determined from the branch tip and inwards as follows, current year (0), one-year-old (1), two-year-old (2) etc. (Fig. 1).

Gas Exchange
Seasonal patterns of the photosynthetic capacity of current- (Y0) and one-year old (Y1) foliage were measured in April, May, July, September, August and October between 2010 and 2013. Influences of canopy position and needle age on photosynthesis were measured for three successive needle cohorts (Y0, Y1 and two-year old (Y2)) from top, middle and bottom branches in July 2011.
• Photosynthetic response (A/Ci) curves were produced using portable infrared gas analyzer systems (LI6400XT, Li-COR, USA). A/Ci curves were generated at saturating light levels (PAR > 1000 μmol m-2 s-1) by sequential adjustment of the reference CO2 concentration between 50 and 1600 ppm (400, 300, 200, 100, 50, 400, 550, 650, 800, 950, 1200 and 1600 ppm) to assess A across a broad range of intercellular CO2 concentrations.
• Temperature response surfaces were generated by replication of the A/Ci curves at multiple temperatures. Cuvette air temperature was regulated from 2 to 50°C by Peltier adjustment of the block temperature and by use of an external temperature controlled circulating water bath attached to the cuvette with block water-jackets (LI-COR model number 6400-88)(Fig. 2). Temperature increments were done in steps of 3-5°C. We measured and included both full (2-50°C) and partial (2-25°C and 20-50°C) temperature series. It took our set-up (Fig. X) c. 5 min to reach target temperature, except at low (2-5°C) and high (40-50°C) temperatures where additional time was needed. We used air temperature here, as the spruce needles were not always in direct contact with the leaf thermocouple, as the case when measuring on broadleaved species. Leaf and air temperature differed on average 0.5°C (ranging from 0.2 to 4.3°C) in the chamber. We minimized variations in VPD by regulating humidity manually (adjusting the scrub). At high temperature we used a compact travel humidifier to increase humidity of the inlet air. Humidity was adjusted prior to, but not during the automated A/Ci curve measurements.
• Temperature responses of foliar daytime Rd were measured in a similar fashion but using a darkened conifer chamber (April and September 2013), but with of several needle cohorts within the same chamber. Rates of respiration were recorded at PAR = 0 μmol m-2 s-1, after the signal had stabilized (typically after 5-10 min).
Following gas exchange measurements, foliage and branch material was shipped on ice to Tennessee, U.S.A. for analysis of leaf area, leaf mass and N content. Shoots were defoliated and projected leaf area (PA) was estimated using WinRHIZO (Regent Instruments Canada Inc., Canada) and ImageJ 1.47 software. Tissue was dried at 70°C then analyzed for leaf N content by mass (Nm) and carbon content using an elemental analyzer (Costech Analytical Technologies, Inc., USA). We calculated nitrogen per leaf area (Na) as Na = Nm × LMA.

Tree Allometry
To estimate canopy foliar mass distribution, eight 4-6 m tall trees were harvested during June/July 2010 and 2011 (Fig. 2A). Each tree was separated by one-meter stem increments and dried, such that foliar mass represented all cohorts of needles within each stem increment. To determine the proportion of total foliar mass represented by each cohort 15 trees were sampled in October 2012. A total of 45 branches were collected at three different positions within the canopy. Foliage on each branch was separated by cohort for analysis of foliar and woody mass, LMA, and N content (Fig. 2B).

Data Analysis
We obtained values for Vcmax, and Jmax for each individual A/Ci curve using the online available platform LeafWeb (http://leafweb.ornl.gov). LeafWeb utilizes the Farquhar-von Caemmerer-Berry method with a novel exhaustive dual optimization approach integrating gm (Gu et al. 2010).
We parameterized the temperature response of Asat, Vcmax and Jmax according to Medlyn et al. (2002) and by fitting eqn. 1 and 2 to gas exchange data collected from Y0 and Y1 needles in August and October.
P(25°C) is the specific parameter (Asat, Vcmax and Jmax) at 25°C (298 K), Ea describes the exponential part of the function or the activation energy, R is the gas constant (8.3143 J K-1 mol-1), and T is air temperature in K, ΔS (J K-1 mol-1) is an entropy term, and Hd (J mol-1) is the deactivation energy. We kept Hd constant at 200 kJ mol-1 to ensure model stability (Medlyn et al. 2002). Equation 2 includes the parameter Topt that is related to ΔS, see Dreyer et al. (2001) and Medlyn et al. (2002) for full method description.
Seasonal, canopy and cohort specific values of Asat, Vcmax and Jmax were normalized to 25°C (Asat25°C, Vcmax25°C and Jmax25°C) by parameterization of eqn. 1, according to season and needle cohort (see table 3 in Jensen et al. 2015). Photosynthetic parameters for Y2 needles were normalized using response of Y1 needles. We make this assumption based on similar photosynthetic capacity of Y1 and Y2 needles in July.
